question: How does the Random Forest algorithm improve upon a single decision tree?

message.content:
Random Forest improves upon a single decision tree primarily by reducing overfitting and increasing predictive stability through ensemble averaging. Instead of relying on one tree’s potentially biased or high-variance structure, the algorithm builds hundreds of trees using two forms of randomness: it trains each tree on a random bootstrap sample of the data, and it considers only a random subset of features at each split. This diversity ensures that the individual trees are de-correlated.

The final prediction is made by aggregating the results of all trees—using majority voting for classification or averaging for regression—which smooths out the noise and errors of any single model. Additionally, Random Forest provides built-in measures of feature importance and performs out-of-bag validation, allowing for robust performance estimation without requiring a separate hold-out test set.
